Triggers.value: Beginning to feel detached or unreal

Maladaptive Strategies.value: keep mind occupied all the time

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

vignette:
Kwame is a 77-year-old software engineer who fled his home country in West Africa during a period of ethnic violence over three decades ago. The event that shattered his life occurred when armed men in uniforms stormed his neighborhood, shouting orders in a language he understood all too well. He was forced to his knees, his hands bound, while they interrogated him about his political affiliations. What he remembers most vividly are not the words, but the images: the glint of a machete held by a man whose face he never saw, the cracked concrete of the courtyard as his cheek pressed against it, the sudden, deafening silence after a gunshot nearby. He recalls these moments as isolated pictures in his mind—a snapshot of a boot, a flash of sunlight on metal, a neighbor's body crumpling—and when he tries to tell his wife about it, he sometimes feels nothing, as if he is describing a scene from a film about a stranger. For years, he pushed these images aside, focusing on his work writing code and raising his family in a quiet American suburb. But now, in retirement, the structure that kept him busy has dissolved, and the pictures have begun to surface unpredictably.

The first time it happened was at a traffic stop. A police officer approached his car and gave him a firm instruction to roll down his window. Kwame’s hands went cold, and his mind flashed to the snapshots of that courtyard—the boot, the machete, the concrete. He fumbled with the window switch, his heart racing, and afterward he could not shake the feeling that the officer’s tone had carried a threat. That evening, as he sat in his living room, he found himself replaying the memory of the gunshot, and the more he tried to push it away, the more insistent the images became. He began to notice that whenever he heard a loud, authoritative voice—a supervisor at a hardware store, a crossing guard directing traffic—his mind would involuntarily snap back to those frozen moments, as if the present command was a key unlocking a door he had kept sealed.

In response, Kwame started to avoid going out altogether. He stopped driving, telling his wife he preferred to walk, but soon he stopped walking too, except for brief trips to the mailbox. He began avoiding other people, crossing the street when he saw a uniform, and declining invitations to community gatherings. To keep his mind occupied, he took to solving complex puzzles on his tablet for hours, losing himself in patterns of numbers and colors so that no room remained for the images. But this strategy backfired: the mental effort exhausted him, and when he finally set the tablet down, the snapshots returned with greater force, as if they had been waiting. The more he avoided going out, the more isolated he became, and the more his memory of the trauma felt like the only vivid thing in his life, outshining the quiet, safe present.

His wife grew worried. She noticed he would flinch when she called his name from another room, and that he had stopped sitting with his back to the door. One afternoon, a delivery driver rang the bell with an urgent knock, and Kwame froze mid-sentence, his eyes fixed on a point in the middle distance. Later, he could not explain why he had felt so terrified, only that the sound had triggered a cascade of images—the shout, the concrete, the silence. The causal chain had become invisible to him: a trigger (authority commands, trauma-related events, even the beginning of a dissociative feeling of unreality) would pull up a memory, the memory would drive him into avoidance or mental distraction, and the avoidance would leave him more vulnerable to the next trigger, each loop tightening the knot.

What finally brought Kwame to seek help was a moment of dissociation in his own kitchen. He was washing dishes when the sun hit the faucet in a certain way, and suddenly he felt detached from his hands, as if he were watching himself from far away. The feeling terrified him more than the memories themselves. He told his wife he needed to talk to someone, though what he fears most is that if he opens the door to those snapshots, he will not be able to close it again. He is hoping, quietly, that someone can help him turn the pictures back into a story he can leave behind.
